explanations.answer: Are You for us or for our enemies
explanations.explanation: Joshua, Israel's leader, asks, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” (Joshua 5:13) He sees a drawn sword and walks UP to it. Me, I'd have asked that question from two counties over, with a megaphone.

explanations.answer: Have You come out from Jericho
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, since Jericho is right there. But Joshua never asks where the man came from. He asks, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” (Joshua 5:13) He wants to know which side the man is on.

explanations.answer: What is Your name and Your people
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like a polite chat at the front door. Joshua skips the small talk. He goes straight to, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” (Joshua 5:13) The man's answer tells Joshua who He is.

Joshua asks, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” and the man answers, “Neither,” (Joshua 5:14). Then He says who He is: “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” So taking Israel's side isn't the answer He gives. I bet Joshua wasn't expecting that one.

Joshua asks if the man is for Israel or for their enemies, and gets one word: “Neither,” (Joshua 5:14). Then the man says, “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” One word, and the whole question gets turned around. I think Joshua stood there a second just taking that in.

The man says, “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” (Joshua 5:14) Joshua responds by falling facedown in reverence. Then he asks, “What does my Lord have to say to His servant?” He knows exactly who he's talking to.

The king of Jericho isn't who this is. The man tells Joshua, “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” (Joshua 5:14) Jericho's king comes up later, when the LORD says He has delivered the city into Joshua's hand, along with its king (Joshua 6:2). In this scene, Joshua falls facedown in reverence.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, never shows up in this scene. The man says plainly, “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” (Joshua 5:14) This Commander answers to the LORD, and Joshua falls facedown in reverence.

The Commander says, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” (Joshua 5:15) Then the text says, “And Joshua did so.” The order and the obeying sit right next to each other. Sandals off, and that's the whole scene.

Laying down a sword is a fair guess, since a drawn sword shows up right at the start, in the Commander's hand (Joshua 5:13). But the Commander never says anything to Joshua about a sword. He says, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” (Joshua 5:15) Sandals are the whole request.
Nobody gets a scrubbing here. The Commander tells Joshua, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” (Joshua 5:15) Washing never comes up, just taking the sandals off.

Not quite, baker. The text says, “Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in.” (Joshua 6:1) That's a city sealed up tight. It's like a bakery with the doors locked, the blinds down, and the sign flipped to CLOSED. Nobody's strolling in, and nobody's strolling out.

Right, those gates are not swinging open. Joshua 6:1 says, “Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in.” Nobody's coming, nobody's going, and nobody's popping out for a quick errand.

Yes! The LORD says, “Behold, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, along with its king and its mighty men of valor.” (Joshua 6:2) The marching directions don't come until the next verse. The LORD hands Joshua the good news before the first lap even starts.

It's the other way around. In Joshua 6:2 the LORD says, “Behold, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, along with its king and its mighty men of valor.” Only after that does He give the marching directions in verse 3. The promise comes first.

The LORD says, “March around the city with all the men of war, circling the city one time. Do this for six days.” (Joshua 6:3) One lap a day. It's about the most relaxed battle plan ever written down.
Two laps would be a little extra, and that's not the plan. Joshua 6:3 says, “…circling the city one time.” That's one lap a day for six days.

Three laps a day would be a workout, but that's not what the LORD says. The plan is “…circling the city one time. Do this for six days.” (Joshua 6:3) A big number of laps does come later, but only on one day.

explanations.answer: They circle the city seven times
explanations.explanation: Six days, one lap each. Then comes the seventh day: “…march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns.” (Joshua 6:4) Joshua 6:15 says that was the only day they circled seven times. Seven laps in one day? Somebody's getting their steps in.

Twice sounds like a gentle step up, but the LORD's plan is bigger. He says, “…on the seventh day, march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns.” (Joshua 6:4) Two laps would barely be a warm-up. Seven is the number.

explanations.answer: They camp and wait at the gates
explanations.explanation: No sitting around at the gates here. The seventh day is still a marching day, and a bigger one: “…march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns.” (Joshua 6:4) The plan never has anyone camping at the gates.
The LORD says, “…have all the people give a mighty shout.” (Joshua 6:5) Not a polite cheer. A mighty one, all the people together.
The LORD says, “Then the wall of the city will collapse…” (Joshua 6:5) It's the wall that comes down. Then the people charge straight in.
A song would be nice, but that's not the word. The LORD says, “…have all the people give a mighty shout.” (Joshua 6:5) Nobody is told to sing in this plan.
A tower isn't what the LORD names. He says, “Then the wall of the city will collapse…” (Joshua 6:5) It's the wall that falls.
Good guess, since gates are how you get into a city. But the LORD doesn't say gate. He says, “Then the wall of the city will collapse…” (Joshua 6:5)

Picture a parade with the ark in the middle. The text says, “…the armed troops marched ahead of the priests who blew the horns, and the rear guard followed the ark.” (Joshua 6:9) Troops, priests, ark, then the rear guard. I bet that spot at the back had a great view of the whole line.
The elders aren't named anywhere in this march. Joshua 6:9 says, “…the rear guard followed the ark.” That's the group at the back of the line.

The text never puts women and children in the march. It says, “…the armed troops marched ahead of the priests who blew the horns, and the rear guard followed the ark.” (Joshua 6:9) The group behind the ark is the rear guard.

explanations.answer: Not one word until he says shout
explanations.explanation: Joshua commands the people, “Do not give a battle cry or let your voice be heard; do not let one word come out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout. Then you are to shout!” (Joshua 6:10) The horns do the sounding. The people have to hold it all in until the day he says.

explanations.answer: Sing praises the whole way around
explanations.explanation: Singing sounds nice, but Joshua's order is different: “Do not give a battle cry or let your voice be heard…” (Joshua 6:10) The text does have the horns sounding during the march (Joshua 6:9). The people are told to keep their voices quiet until the day he says to shout. That's a lot of holding it in.

explanations.answer: Call on the city to surrender
explanations.explanation: Nobody is told to call anything out to Jericho. Joshua says, “do not let one word come out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout.” (Joshua 6:10) That means no words at all, surrender or otherwise.

Yes. The text says, “So he had the ark of the LORD carried around the city, circling it once. And the people returned to the camp and spent the night there.” (Joshua 6:11) One lap, then back to camp for the night. Then they got up and did it again the next day. That's some serious patience, and I know how hard waiting is. I once waited in a junk drawer for years.

This one is true, baker. Joshua 6:11 says, “And the people returned to the camp and spent the night there.” That comes right after the one lap around the city. I think it's easy to second-guess, since marching around a city feels like it should take longer.

The horns keep blowing. Joshua 6:13 says, “…the seven priests carrying seven rams’ horns kept marching ahead of the ark of the LORD and blowing the horns.” It's the people who stay silent, not the horns. Same plan as the first day.
That's right. On the second day, “…the horns kept sounding.” (Joshua 6:13) The priests keep blowing while they march. The people are the ones under orders to keep quiet.

The text says, “Then on the seventh day, they got up at dawn and marched around the city seven times in the same manner.” (Joshua 6:15) It's an early start for a lot of laps. I'd be hitting snooze like it owed me money.
Noon would be a late start for a seven-lap day. The text says they “…got up at dawn…” (Joshua 6:15) They started early.

Midnight is a fun guess, but the text says dawn. Joshua 6:15 says, “…they got up at dawn and marched around the city seven times in the same manner.” Dawn is when the day is just starting, not the middle of the night. Marching seven laps in the pitch dark would be a whole different kind of rough.

explanations.answer: Rahab and all those with her
explanations.explanation: Joshua says, “Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent.” (Joshua 6:17) The text gives her reason: she hid the spies. Everyone with her in her house is included. That's a house worth being in.

explanations.answer: Tamar and all those with her
explanations.explanation: Tamar's a real name in the Bible, baker, but she's not in this story. She's the Tamar who shows up in Genesis 38:6. Joshua says, “Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent.” (Joshua 6:17) Rahab is the one who hid the spies, and that's the reason the text gives. Her house is the one that gets spared.

explanations.answer: Deborah and all those with her
explanations.explanation: Deborah shows up later in the Bible as a judge (Judges 4:4), but she has no part in Jericho. Listen to who Joshua names: Rahab, the woman who hid the spies. Her whole household was spared, “…all those with her in her house…” (Joshua 6:17) That's a lot of people covered by one brave choice.
Joshua says Rahab lives “…because she hid the spies we sent.” (Joshua 6:17) The text gives that as her reason. She hid them, and she and her house are spared.
Feeding the spies isn't what the text says. Joshua says Rahab lives “…because she hid the spies we sent.” (Joshua 6:17) The word is hid.
No money changes hands in this verse. Joshua says Rahab lives “…because she hid the spies we sent.” (Joshua 6:17) What she did was hide them.

Not quite. Joshua says, “…all the silver and gold and all the articles of bronze and iron are holy to the LORD; they must go into His treasury.” (Joshua 6:19) Nobody gets to pocket any of it. It all belongs to the LORD.

Right, no souvenirs. Joshua says, “…all the silver and gold and all the articles of bronze and iron are holy to the LORD; they must go into His treasury.” (Joshua 6:19) He also warns, “…keep away from the things devoted to destruction…” (Joshua 6:18)

explanations.answer: The two men who spied out the land
explanations.explanation: Joshua tells “…the two men who had spied out the land…” to go into the house of the prostitute and bring out the woman and all who are with her. (Joshua 6:22) His words even include “…just as you promised her.” So the text shows the spies getting the job, and a promise to Rahab is part of the order. I think that fits nicely.

explanations.answer: The seven priests with the horns
explanations.explanation: The priests do have a job in this passage: seven of them carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark (Joshua 6:4). But Joshua gives this errand to someone else: “…the two men who had spied out the land…” (Joshua 6:22) The text doesn't send any priests to Rahab's house.

explanations.answer: The rear guard behind the ark
explanations.explanation: The rear guard followed the ark during the march (Joshua 6:9), but this job doesn't go to them. Joshua tells “…the two men who had spied out the land…” to go bring Rahab out. (Joshua 6:22) They were the ones who made the promise.

The text says the spies “…brought out her whole family and settled them outside the camp of Israel.” (Joshua 6:23) So the word that matters here is outside. The spies brought out Rahab, her father and mother and brothers, and all who belonged to her. Inside the camp isn't where the text puts them.
Yes. Joshua 6:23 says the spies “…brought out her whole family and settled them outside the camp of Israel.” Outside the camp is where the text puts them. It adds nothing more about why.
The text says, “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day.” (Joshua 6:25) Rahab ended up living with Israel. The writer says that was still true as he wrote.

The Moabites are another people, and they're not in this verse. Joshua 6:25 says, “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day.” That tells us where Rahab's life ended up, which is with Israel. The writer says it was still true as he wrote.
The Egyptians aren't who this verse is talking about. It says, “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day.” (Joshua 6:25) Her new home is with Israel.

explanations.answer: He is cursed before the LORD
explanations.explanation: Joshua says, “Cursed before the LORD is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho…” (Joshua 6:26) That's a solemn oath. It's a serious one, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: He is blessed with a great name
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Joshua says. His oath begins, “Cursed before the LORD is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho…” (Joshua 6:26) Nothing about a great name.

explanations.answer: He will rule over all the land
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the oath promises him a throne. Joshua says, “Cursed before the LORD is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho…” (Joshua 6:26) It's a curse, not a crown.

Yes. Joshua says, “at the cost of his firstborn he will lay its foundations; at the cost of his youngest he will set up its gates.” (Joshua 6:26) The oath is about the man who rises up and rebuilds Jericho. This one is heavy, so I'll just let it stand as written.

This one is true, and it's a heavy one. Joshua's oath says, “at the cost of his firstborn he will lay its foundations; at the cost of his youngest he will set up its gates.” (Joshua 6:26) Firstborn is right there in the text.

Yes. The text says, “So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land.” (Joshua 6:27) Both things sit in that one verse. Joshua's name got around the whole land. I think the part to hold onto is the first one, that the LORD was with him.
This one is true, friend. Joshua 6:27 says, “So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land.” Word about him got around everywhere.
